title: Motifs et théorie de Hodge : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction: The page is not a Grothendieck manuscript page. It is a typed or stencilled sheet headed '-VII- 19 -' and 'n°383', titled 'Système de racines de type G2', inserted into the folder. The number 59 in pencil is the archive pagination. Its format looks like a Bourbaki-style rédaction or planche, but that attribution is unsure. It shows the 12 roots of G2 drawn from the origin O. Two simple roots are marked 'simple': α1 is short and horizontal; α2 is long, at 150° to α1. Dashed lines build the positive roots as successive sums: α2, α2+α1, α2+2α1, α2+3α1, and 2α2+3α1, which is labelled 'plus grande racine'. The negatives are drawn as unlabelled endpoints. In coordinates α1=(1,0) and α2=(-3/2, √3/2). Then α2+α1=(-1/2, √3/2) and α2+2α1=(1/2, √3/2) are short. α2+3α1=(3/2, √3/2) and 2α2+3α1=(0, √3) are long. This matches the figure: six short and six long roots, length ratio √3, with long roots at angles 30°, 90°, 150° and so on. In context, the surrounding notes (pp. 58 and 60) treat the Galois image φ_v: Gal(k/k0) → G(k) of a motive and the Zariski density of its image in the motivic, Mumford–Tate-type group G. The neighbouring pages do not themselves name G2. So the most likely reason the sheet sits here is that Grothendieck wanted a concrete reductive group, such as G2, as a test case for which groups can occur as motivic Galois groups. That reading is a conjecture about the folder's assembly, not something written on the page.

ideas.what: Root system of G2 with simple roots α1 (short) and α2 (long), and positive roots α1, α2, α1+α2, 2α1+α2, 3α1+α2, 3α1+2α2 (highest root)
ideas.modern_name: G2 root system / positive roots and highest root
ideas.usually_credited_to: Killing, É. Cartan; standard presentation in Bourbaki, Groupes et algèbres de Lie, ch. VI (Planche IX)

missed.claim: This is a possible, speculative contextual link only. A G2 root-system sheet is filed among notes on motivic Galois groups and the Zariski density of Galois images (pp. 58 and 60). That might suggest Grothendieck considered exceptional groups like G2 as candidate motivic or Mumford–Tate groups. The question 'is G2 a motivic Galois group?' was later raised explicitly by Serre and answered by Dettweiler–Reiter (2010) and others. The page itself contains no such statement.
missed.quote: Système de racines de type G2
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only as minor historical evidence of early interest in exceptional motivic Galois groups. Nothing mathematical is new.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a standard typed figure of the G2 root system, probably a reference sheet from a Bourbaki-type document. It is correct and routine; at most its placement in the motives folder is of mild historical interest.
transcription_corrections: The 'o' near the centre is the origin label O (or 0), not text.
'59' is the archive's pencil pagination, not part of the content.
The faint words 'simple' (under α2, beside α1) and '(plus grande racine)' are lighter typewriter or stencil text and belong to the figure.
The sheet is typed or stencilled ('-VII- 19 -', 'n°383'), not handwritten by Grothendieck.
